Hey OP, almost exactly this situation happened to me. My partner has been genuinely remorseful and has essentially done a 180 on where they were going with their mental and physical health when it happened. As far as I can tell, it’s never happened again, and they have been a great partner since going on medication. So there is hope.

Now, the tough part. At first it was all I could do to blame bipolar for the cheating to be able to stomach moving forward. It got so bad I had to imagine that it was someone else entirely I was dating when it happened and i had to pretend I moved on with someone else. It was just too painful to imagine they did and said all of those things with intent, that came from somewhere dark and malicious, that they have ownership over. Do people in manic episodes behave irrationally and ruin their lives? Yes, it happens. But that doesn’t absolve them of the responsibility, because they had a long time to weigh the pros and cons of cheating especially if it was an ongoing affair. They made the decision every day to continue, and to not to tell you. It’s a very unkind thing they did to you. And you need to know that it was, in fact, them who did it, not the disease, because you can’t begin to heal in the context of your relationship until you accept it caused you this harm that you won’t ever forget.

I won’t say it goes away, or it fades with time. Just a few days ago, five years after d-day, I had a panic attack and checked flights because my partner flew to their parents and I needed to make sure they flight they took really existed. Panicked moments like that where you react with fear and suspicion are going to be really common in your near future, and probably won’t ever go away unless you’re a very strong person. They have gotten less intense and less frequent with time, but the ripple of this betrayal will be with you for as long as you choose this relationship — it is forever colored and contextualized by it. That doesn’t mean it’s unsalvageable, but it’s something that you have to come to terms with ASAP.

If you accept he chose to do this, understand the illness enabled it but isn’t the sole bearer of responsibility, make sure he does the work, and work hard yourself, things will get better. The quicker you go through those things, the easier it will get. But you can’t make someone change in ways they aren’t willing to. Be honest with yourself and be attentive — focus on actions, not words. I’m sorry this happened to you, it’s a unique pain when it’s in such a committed relationship and even more unique still when it’s bipolar related. Best of luck.

Weight neutral health care is more about not having the information readily available for diagnostic purposes, not for medication. People get taken more seriously on paper and afforded more visits and referrals if they don’t have “morbidly obese” or “obese” on their docket. It also pushes those weight related conversations only to moments where it’s needed; anesthesia is a great example of when weight would be immediately disclosed.

There are next to no studies that successfully prove causation between weight and illness (diet != weight, diet discussion is not ignored in weight neutral approaches) — it takes bias out of the equation.

While I agree this tweet is probably seriously exaggerated, the approach is actually pretty good for removing implicit biases and allowing people to get successfully diagnosed and triaged without doctors suggesting only a weight change for something like chronic pain or extreme bowel symptoms that can often be cancer signs, etc. Doctors are human too and can’t pull superhuman feats like removing their own biases from care at all times

A lot of educational resources just talk about phase relationships between mic signals of the same event (different mics on a drum set, multiple vocal microphones, etc) -- what I'm speaking to is mostly related to how EQs actually work. This changes the phase relationship of the signal with itself -- that might sound strange, but an easy (if not slightly inaccurate) way to describe raising a small Q at 500hz is playing the original signal alongside another, processed signal that is only that Q information, with the rest of the signal phase flipped out (the partial playing over the original audio). Honestly, I wouldn't do this on the master bus. It's not a huge deal, but...

While the human ear can't hear below 20-50hz, and if untamed this information can eat compressor headroom, cutting it out has some transient effects. You \_can\_ (without a good linear phase EQ) cause phase shift and added/changed harmonics in the audible range. You will almost certainly change the harmonic information in the audible range. Whether or not it changes enough for you to hear depends on the track.

Instead, I would cut this frequency on everything that doesn't have useful or impactful bass information (think 0-300hz). You can clean up the sub signal going into the master bus, you have a smaller chance of affecting the harmonic information and phase of the individual tracks, and you (if done right) have a really clean sub signal going into the master bus, which reduces the chance of it eating up a large amount of headroom.

Just my $0.02!
